claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially a homogeneous high-temperature BCC phase.
Phase evolution during cooling and thermal exposure is governed by differential diffusion of key elements.
Al and Cr are especially important to the proposed differential-diffusion process.
Differential diffusion produces local compositional fluctuations and segregation.
Local compositional fluctuations and segregation drive nucleation of secondary ordered phases from the BCC matrix.
The secondary phases may include B2-type phases or other intermetallics.
Slow cooling or intermediate-temperature annealing permits more elemental diffusion and segregation than rapid quenching.
Diffusion-driven compositional fluctuations may develop at grain boundaries or within grains.
Al, and possibly Cr, diffuse relatively rapidly during slow cooling or intermediate thermal exposure.
Local segregation alters the chemical composition and thermodynamic landscape.
The altered local thermodynamic landscape drives ordering or phase separation within the BCC matrix.
Slow-cooled or annealed specimens will contain detectable secondary phases alongside residual BCC.
Rapidly quenched specimens will largely retain a metastable homogeneous BCC structure with minimal segregation.
The proposed mechanism applies when cooling or annealing provides enough time and temperature for significant diffusion and segregation.
The proposed mechanism should not operate during an extremely rapid quench or at temperatures too low to activate diffusion.
Under diffusion-suppressing conditions, the alloy should remain homogeneous.
The exact identity, morphology, and volume fraction of the secondary phases may depend on processing and local composition.
A lack of any significant phase-constitution or segregation difference between quenched and slowly cooled or annealed samples would falsify the hypothesis.
